unions.comment:
Shadow tilemap for text windows (WRAM bank $05). The same 32 x 32 cell
plane plus CGB attribute plane the full-screen UIs keep in WRAM bank
$03, but owned by the window engine: ResetTextWindowState clears both
and points wShadowTilemapPtr / wShadowTilemapBank at $d000 / $05, and
the dirty-row flusher copies changed rows out to $9800.
Scoped to a provable WRAM bank $05 alone -- bank $05 is full of $d000
and $d400 literals that address whichever plane the current screen
owns, and its glyph buffers live at $d300-$d7ff in WRAM bank $07.
The one instruction range is the exception RestoreShadowTilemapRow forces:
it reads a row out of wMapBuffer64 under WRAM banks $03 and $02 and writes
it back into these planes under bank $05, so the bank live at the `ld hl,
$d400` is the source's, not the destination's.

0xd000.name: wWindowShadowTilemap
0xd000.note: Tile plane of the text-window shadow tilemap: 32 x 32 cells, rows TILEMAP_WIDTH apart, of which the top-left 20 x 18 is on screen

0xd400.name: wWindowShadowAttrmap
0xd400.note: CGB attribute plane of the text-window shadow tilemap, cell for cell with wWindowShadowTilemap and copied to $9800 in VRAM bank 1

unions.comment:
Window bookkeeping (WRAM bank $05), owned by the bank $05 window system:
the window struct array, the dirty-row flags that drive the shadow
tilemap flush, and the allocator mask above them. Scoped to bank $05
in two ranges rather than one, because WriteStringToTilemapStreamed at
$6bf0-$6c4f keeps its own cursor at $dc05-$dc0a in *the caller's* WRAM
bank -- it writes glyphs straight to a tilemap the caller selected --
so those bytes are not windows and stay numeric. Banks $0d and $17/$3b
overlay the same addresses in WRAM banks $04 and $03 (separate unions).

0xdc00.name: wWindowStructs
0xdc00.note:
[64 bytes] Eight 8-byte window records, indexed by window id (GetWindowStructPtr masks the id to 3 bits and shifts left 3):
  +$00 column, +$01 row (both wrapped to $1f by SetWindowRect)
  +$02 height in cells, +$03 width in cells
  +$04 state, read and written through GetWindowState / SetWindowState
  +$06 text id (lo/hi), stored by SetWindowTextId; $03 in the high byte
       is the "no text" sentinel RenderWindowText bails on
AllocWindowStruct fills a free slot from de/bc, FreeWindow zeroes all
eight bytes and releases the wWindowSlotMask bit

0xdc40.name: wTilemapRowDirty
0xdc40.note: [32 bytes] One flag per tilemap row. SetRowDirtyFlags clears the array and marks the e rows starting at d (wrapping at 32), which is how a window redraw tells the flusher which rows changed

0xdc60.name: wTilemapRowRuns
0xdc60.note: [16 bytes] Run list BuildDirtyRowRuns folds wTilemapRowDirty into: (first row, run length) pairs terminated by $ff, with runs capped at 7 rows so one FlushDirtyRowsPerFrame pass fits in a VBlank. The flusher copies each run and waits a frame between them

0xdc70.name: wWindowSlotMask
0xdc70.note: [8-bit] One bit per window struct, set while the slot is in use. AllocWindowSlotBit scans for a clear bit and claims it; FreeWindow clears it again

0xdc76.name: wShadowTilemapReadOffset
0xdc76.note: [16-bit] Byte offset added to wShadowTilemapPtr by RefreshShadowTilemapFromMapBuffer when it copies rows back to the shadow tilemap. Nothing ever writes it, so it stays at the 0 ResetTextWindowState leaves behind

0xdc78.name: wSavedWindowStruct
0xdc78.note: [8 bytes] Scratch copy of one window record. SaveWindowStruct parks the struct here so a routine can rewrite the live one and still compare against where the window started -- OpenSpeechBubble walks the bubble outward one cell at a time against the saved column

unions.comment:
Text and dialogue engine state (WRAM bank $05), owned by the bank $05
text/window engine and driven from the bank $0a story scripts and the
bank $0b drill messages. Scoped to those three ROM banks as well as to
the WRAM bank, because the engine selects bank $05 once on entry and
then saves and restores an unknown bank around its glyph-buffer work,
so compute_wram_bank cannot prove it at every reference.
The scope is not decoration: bank $1b keeps its ranking-marker
animation channels over the same $d84x bytes in a different WRAM bank,
and banks $18/$1a/$6b address $d8bx/$d8fx as screen tilemap cells.

0xd841.name: wTextArrowBlinkCounter
0xd841.note: [8-bit] Frame counter for the menu-cursor arrow blink task; bit 4 selects the tile it writes ($20 blank / $0d arrow)

0xd842.name: wTextArrowCell
0xd842.note: [16-bit] Shadow-tilemap address of the cell the cursor arrow sits in. AnimateTextArrowTask turns it into a VRAM address (+ $3000 + $9800) and blinks the arrow there; RunMenuSelection primes it to $ffff and rewrites it every time the cursor moves

0xd844.name: wTextArrowEraseAddr
0xd844.note: [16-bit] VRAM address of the cell the arrow just left, handed to the blink task to overwrite with tile $20. The task clears it once erased, so a zero here is also how it knows nothing is pending -- AnimateTextArrowTask tests the low byte, AnimateMenuScrollArrowsTask the high one

0xd846.name: wMenuPage
0xd846.note: [8-bit] Page RunPagedTextMenu is showing; left/right step it and wrap against the page count. The entry it returns is wMenuPage * 4 + the row picked, so each page holds four rows

0xd847.name: wTextArgStringWriteIndex
0xd847.note: [8-bit] Cursor into wTextArgStringQueue: PushTextArgString writes at it, TextCmdPrintArgString reads at it, and the dialogue entry points reset it to 0 between messages. Stops at 16

0xd848.name: wTextArgNumberWriteIndex
0xd848.note: [8-bit] The same cursor for wTextArgNumberQueue, shared by PushTextArgNumber and TextCmdPrintArgNumber

0xd849.name: wTextArgShortTextWriteIndex
0xd849.note: [8-bit] The same cursor for wTextArgShortTextQueue, written by PushTextArgShortTextId

0xd84a.name: wTextArgStringCount
0xd84a.note: [8-bit] How many string args were pushed. Kept in step with wTextArgStringWriteIndex while queuing and left alone when the cursor is reset, which is what makes it the limit the print command stops at

0xd84b.name: wTextArgNumberCount
0xd84b.note: [8-bit] The same count for wTextArgNumberQueue; TextCmdPrintArgNumber prints nothing once the cursor reaches it

0xd84e.name: wTextResumePtr
0xd84e.note: [16-bit] Text-stream pointer to pick up from instead of the start of wTextBuffer, with a nonzero high byte as the "set" flag that RenderTextString and FitWindowToText test and then clear. Two producers fill it: TextCmdWaitButtonPage makes TextInterpreterLoop store the byte it stopped on, and FindDialogueChoiceMarker stores the position of the $02 choice marker so the yes/no prompt measures and renders only the tail

0xd850.name: wTextPageBreakRequest
0xd850.note: [8-bit] Set by TextCmdWaitButtonPage; TextInterpreterLoop saves the resume offset to wTextResumePtr and returns, and the dialogue loops keep re-entering while it is set

0xd851.name: wDialogueSpeaker
0xd851.note: [8-bit] Who the current dialogue belongs to, as passed to ShowSpeakerDialogue ($ff becomes 0). Bit 7 set means the low bits are a literal screen row; clear means they are an actor id, and OpenSpeechBubble / ShowYesNoPromptWindow read that actor's Y against the camera to decide whether the window opens on the top or the bottom half of the screen

0xd852.name: wScriptDialogueTextId
0xd852.note: [16-bit] Text id the story script is up to. InitDialogueTextCursor seeds it and every Script*Dialogue call in bank $0a shows it and increments, so a cutscene walks a run of consecutive ids without naming each one

0xd854.name: wFitTextWidthCells
0xd854.note: [8-bit] Widest line of the measured text, rounded up to whole cells -- FitWindowToText writes it, MeasureDialogueWidthTiles returns it

0xd85c.name: wSpeechBubbleLowerHalf
0xd85c.note: [8-bit] 1 when OpenSpeechBubble / OpenCenteredDialogueWindow put the window on the lower half of the screen because the speaking actor is near the top, 0 otherwise. Written by both, read by nothing

0xd85d.name: wUnusedTextByte
0xd85d.note: [8-bit] The byte Unused_05_SetTextVar stores. Nothing reads it

0xd85f.name: wWindowTextEmpty
0xd85f.note: [8-bit] Set to 1 when RenderWindowText bails because the window's text id has $03 in its high byte (the "no text" sentinel), 0 when it goes on to fetch and render. Written by nothing else and read by nothing

0xd862.name: wDialogueVoice
0xd862.note: [8-bit] Speaker voice for the per-character text blip: DelayTextCharacter plays sound $9a + voice * 4 + (glyph & 3) as each glyph lands. GetSpeakerVoice supplies it, and $08 means silent -- which is also what a negative message speed forces

0xd863.name: wFixedMenuWindowId
0xd863.note: [8-bit] Window SetFixedMenuWindowTextId built, so RunFixedTextMenu can close it alongside the menu window. Both are exported through the bank $05 farptr table and neither is called, which is just as well: SetFixedMenuWindowTextId loads hWramBank into b before calling SetWindowTextId, so the "window id" both routines pass around is really the WRAM bank number

0xd864.name: wGlyphVramDest
0xd864.note: [16-bit] Current VRAM destination address for glyph tiles (lo/hi)

0xd866.name: wTextArgStringMeasureIndex
0xd866.note: [8-bit] Second cursor into wTextArgStringQueue, stepped by MeasureNextArgStringWidth. FitWindowToText walks the whole message to size the window before a glyph is drawn, so the measure pass needs its own cursor per queue; the dialogue entry points reset all six together

0xd867.name: wTextArgNumberMeasureIndex
0xd867.note: [8-bit] The measure-pass cursor into wTextArgNumberQueue, stepped by MeasureNextArgNumberWidth

0xd868.name: wTextArgShortTextMeasureIndex
0xd868.note: [8-bit] The measure-pass cursor into wTextArgShortTextQueue, stepped by GetNextArgShortTextLength

0xd869.name: wTextStreamPtr
0xd869.note: [16-bit] Current read pointer into the text byte stream

0xd86f.name: wFitTextLineCount
0xd86f.note: [8-bit] Number of lines the measured text came to, the companion of wFitTextWidthCells. ShowDrillMessageByIndex turns it into a window height of lines * 2 + 1

unions.comment:
Short-text scratch buffer (WRAM bank $05). Scoped wider than the rest of
the text engine because the copy into it lives in the text banks: every
bank that holds strings ends with the same FetchShortText tail, and it
is that tail, not the engine, that names $d880. The bank $6b intro
cutscene addresses the same bytes as tilemap rows in WRAM banks $03/$04,
which is what the scope keeps out.

0xd880.name: wShortTextBuffer
0xd880.note: [16 bytes] Short string buffer: the text-bank fetch routines copy the string here instead of into wTextBuffer when called with a != 0

unions.comment:
Text-argument queues (WRAM bank $05): three parallel 16-entry rings the
text control codes pop from, each with a cursor, a count and a second
cursor for the measuring pass at $d847-$d84c / $d866-$d868. Same scope as
the $d841 block -- banks $18/$1a/$1b/$6b address these bytes as screen
tilemap cells in other WRAM banks.

0xd8b0.name: wTextArgStringQueue
0xd8b0.note: 16 x 2-byte string pointers queued by PushTextArgString. The high nibble carries a WRAM bank tag, so an argument can point into a banked buffer

0xd8d0.name: wTextArgNumberQueue
0xd8d0.note: 16 x 2-byte values queued by PushTextArgNumber for TextCmdPrintArgNumber

0xd8f0.name: wTextArgShortTextQueue
0xd8f0.note: 16 x 1-byte short-text ids queued by PushTextArgShortTextId; the $08 control code pops one and prints the string it names

unions.comment:
Where the shared HRAM pool goes during an audio update (WRAM bank $07).
Scoped to RunSoundEngine itself: bank $05 and the boot path also load
$d000 with WRAM bank $07 selected, and there it is the base of a
4 KiB clear over the whole bank, not this buffer.

0xd000.name: wSndHramSave
0xd000.note: [32 bytes] Copy of $ffd0-$ffef taken by RunSoundEngine on entry and put back on exit. The driver keeps its channel state in that HRAM window, so context-switching it is what lets four other subsystems keep their own bytes there across an audio update -- see the $ffd0 union

unions.comment:
Two subsystems overlay this 2 KiB of WRAM bank $07. The text engine keeps
its glyph tiles here and uploads them to VRAM $8800; the bank $03 save
engine borrows the same bytes as block staging, because a save never runs
while text is being composed.
Both constraints are needed on every scope. The WRAM bank alone cannot
separate the two overlays -- an interior byte would take whichever symbol
was registered first -- and the ROM bank alone is far too coarse: a 2 KiB
extent would otherwise claim every $d3xx-$dafx literal in banks $05/$3f,
which is most of the window engine and two decompression buffers in other
WRAM banks.
Bank $03's debug save editor loads $d300 as well -- it hex-dumps the whole
region from there, one byte at a time under a cursor, so that literal is a
window base rather than a variable and is left numeric. (Its "wipe the
block" branch clears from $d300 and its slot-3 branch edits $d300+, both
$200 short of where ReadCurrentSlotBlock actually puts the block.)

0xd300.name: wGlyphTileBuffer
0xd300.note: [2048 bytes] 128 proportional-font glyph tiles, laid out 1:1 against VRAM $8800 so tile n is at + n * TILE_SIZE and uploads to $8800 + n * TILE_SIZE. ClearGlyphBuffer fills all 128 with the blank glyph; UploadGlyphBufferFull sends the first 80 as five 256-byte pages, and UploadGlyphTilesPartial / UploadGlyphTileRange send narrower runs

0xd480.name: wMinigameRecordBlock
0xd480.note: [32 bytes] Image of a minigame-record save block ($38 + story slot): 16 16-bit records indexed by record id. ReadMinigameRecord zeroes it, reads the block over it and hands record b back through wMinigameRecordValue; WriteMinigameRecord does the reverse and verifies the block afterwards

0xd500.name: wSaveBlockBuffer
0xd500.note: [512 bytes] Image of whichever $200-byte block the save engine is working on: the story slot block for ReadCurrentSlotBlock / WriteCurrentSlotBlock (ids from StorySlotBlockIds_03), and block $0b for the N64 transfer records. ApplyN64RecordsUnlockFlags and UpdateUnlockablesSaveBlock address the unlock bytes at +$00-$07 directly

unions.comment:
The scene's two cell maps, WRAM bank $06: what each half-tile of the
overworld collides with, and what behaviour it triggers. Both are
decompressed by LoadStorySceneGraphics (and its sibling at $5d8e), which
selects WRAM bank $06 and then fills $d400 and $d000 in that order.
GetCollisionMapCellAddr and GetBehaviorMapCellAddr index them with the same
arithmetic -- 32 columns of half-tiles, rows 32 apart -- and their four
ReadRead/Write wrappers select bank $06 around the single load or store, so
the reference itself sits under WRAM bank $04 (the actor engine's) and the
two bases would otherwise render as wActors and wActors + 16 * ACTOR_SIZE.
Declared mirrored so it names these bytes without allocating them: WRAM bank
$06 already declares this range for the character-data screen and the
palette fade engine, and the overworld simply owns it at another time.

0xd000.name: wCollisionMap
0xd000.note: [1024 bytes] One byte per half-tile cell of the scene, 32 columns by 32 rows, addressed as (y & ~1) * 16 + (x & ~1) / 2 by GetCollisionMapCellAddr. ReadCollisionMapCell and WriteCollisionMapCell are the only accessors, each selecting WRAM bank $06 for the one instruction that touches it.

0xd400.name: wBehaviorMap
0xd400.note: [1024 bytes] The second plane of the same grid, cell for cell $400 higher, holding what a cell does rather than whether it blocks. ReadBehaviorMapCell prints the byte it reads with PrintHexByte, which is what makes it visible as a debug readout.

unions.comment:
Overworld / story actor slots (WRAM bank $04): 24 records of ACTOR_SIZE
bytes, the array SpawnActor allocates from and the bank $04 engine walks
once a frame. Scoped to a provable WRAM bank $04 -- $d000 is eight
different things and seven ROM banks reach the array, so nothing but the
dataflow can say which one a literal means.
Two bank $0a sites get instruction ranges instead, because there the bank
is selected in the callee and never at the reference: GetActorStateAddr
builds its slot address and only then runs `wram_bank $04`, and
EndCutsceneScriptMode hands slots 1 and 0 to AttachActorWaypointFollower,
which selects the bank itself.
Record fields are addressed as offsets (`ld hl, $00xx / add hl, bc`), not
as absolute addresses, so they are not RAM symbols; the layout is in
docs/actor_script.md and the field-size table the script opcodes use is
ActorFieldTypeTable_04.

scopes.note: WaitPlayerMoveDone loads the slot-1 pointer and only selects WRAM bank $04 two instructions later, so the bank observed at the operand is the caller's, not the one it means

0xd000.name: wActors
0xd000.note: [24 x ACTOR_SIZE] Actor slots. +$00 script pointer, +$02 its bank, +$03 wait counter, +$05 flags (bit 0 paused, bit 7 moving), +$08/+$0a move target, +$0c/+$0e position, +$21 object id, +$30 flags (bit 7 = live), +$32 facing. A slot is free when +$01 is zero

unions.comment:
List of actor slots near the player (WRAM bank $04), rebuilt by
BuildNearbyActorList. Scoped to the bank $04 actor engine as well as to
the WRAM bank: banks $18/$1b/$28/$38 keep unrelated screen state at the
same addresses in WRAM bank $03.

0xda00.name: wNearbyActorList
0xda00.note: [up to 24 x 2 bytes + terminator] Pointers to the live actor slots BuildNearbyActorList selected -- those with a nonzero +$01, +$30 bit 7 set and +$05 bit 3 set, close enough to the player. A zero word ends the list, which is how FindActorAtPoint and the proximity searches stop

unions.comment:
Actor-engine staging buffers (WRAM bank $04), owned by bank $04. Two ROM
records are copied through here rather than read in place, because both
live in whichever bank the caller was running and the engine wants them
at a fixed address.

0xdac0.name: wActorTemplate
0xdac0.note: [14 bytes] One map_actor record, copied out of the ROM list by SpawnActorsFromList and handed to SpawnActorFromTemplate. +$09 (the obj_id byte) reads $ff on the entry that terminates the list

0xdad0.name: wActorObjDef
0xdad0.note: [16 bytes] The object-definition record LoadActorObjectDef copies in from the ObjectIdList_04 entry, then distributes into the slot: +$00 to +$37, +$01 to +$35, +$04/+$05 to +$24, +$06/+$07 to +$28, +$0a/+$0b to +$38, and +$08 as a far pointer to palette data when +$00 came out $63. The palette path reuses the first 8 bytes as the copy destination

0xdae0.name: wActorScreenOriginX
0xdae0.note: [16-bit] Negated camera X plus screen shake, recomputed each frame. DrawActorSprite adds it to an actor position to get a screen coordinate, which is why it is stored already negated

0xdae2.name: wActorScreenOriginY
0xdae2.note: [16-bit] The same for Y, from wCameraY and wScreenShakeOffsetY (plus the $cb02 offset while the ending credits run)

0xdae9.name: wPlayerObjDefPending
0xdae9.note: [8-bit] Cleared by SetPlayerActorObjectDef before it reloads actor 0's object definition. Nothing reads it

unions.comment:
Working copy of the minigame target actor being updated (WRAM bank $04),
the same pattern as wObjSlotWork: UpdateMinigameTarget copies the slot in,
runs its script, movement, draw and hit checks against this one fixed
record, and copies it back. Owned by bank $0a.

0xdcf0.name: wMinigameTargetWork
0xdcf0.note: [16 bytes] +$00 flags (bit 0 live, bit 1 moving toward the goal), +$02 delay counter the update ticks down, +$06/+$08 current position, +$0a/+$0c goal position. MoveMinigameTargetTowardGoal steps the current position toward the goal $10 units at a time

unions.comment:
Two screens over the same 40 bytes of WRAM bank $03: bank $38 keeps the
character-unlock array here and bank $1b its ranking-banner animation.
The array runs straight through where the banner bytes sit, so they are
variants of one union rather than two unions side by side.

0xd840.name: wCharUnlockFlags
0xd840.note: [40 bytes] One byte per character, nonzero when unlocked. BuildCharUnlockFlags clears the array and walks CharUnlockFlagsTable0, marking a character either because its entry reads $ffff (always available) or because TestSaveFlag says so. PackUnlockFlagsForLink folds eight at a time into one bit each for the link exchange

0xd840.name: wRankingAnimSlotPtrs
0xd840.note: [4 x 16-bit] One pointer per animation channel to the ranking marker slot that channel moves, stored from hl by StartRankingMarkerAnim<N> (the callers get it from GetRankingMarkerSlot). UpdateScriptedOffsetChannel<N> reloads it each frame and adds the script's delta to the slot's +1 on channels 0 and 1 and to its +2 on channels 2 and 3 -- the X and Y DrawRankingMarkersTask hands to QueueSprite as d and e

0xd848.name: wRankingAnimScriptPtrs
0xd848.note: [4 x 16-bit] One pointer per channel to the delta script it is playing, stored from de by StartRankingMarkerAnim<N>. A script is one byte of movement per frame -- $01 or $ff in every table here -- ending at $40, which is UpdateScriptedOffsetChannel<N>'s cue to unregister its own frame task rather than a delta

0xd850.name: wRankingAnimStepIndex
0xd850.note: [4 bytes] How far into its script each channel is. StartRankingMarkerAnim<N> zeroes its byte; UpdateScriptedOffsetChannel<N> reads the script at this offset and, unless it was the $40 terminator, increments it -- so the byte is the frame counter as well as the index

0xd855.name: wRankingBannerAnimFrame
0xd855.note: [8-bit] Frame counter for the sliding banner sprite. RankingBoardAnimTask_1b indexes RankingBoardAnimTaskTable with it for this frame's X delta, and unregisters itself once it reaches $87

0xd856.name: wRankingBannerX
0xd856.note: [8-bit] X the banner sprite is drawn at, seeded to $a0 on frame 0 and advanced by the table delta every frame after

0xd858.name: wRankingAnimStateDone
0xd858.note: [8-bit] Set to 1 at the end of each ranking-board animation state, which is how the state machine knows the current step has played out

0xd85a.name: wRankingBoardSilent
0xd85a.note: [8-bit] Set when ShowRankingBoard is called with mode $03, which it then rewrites to $00. It suppresses the board's entrance animation (DispatchRankingBoardAnim returns at once) and the closing jingle -- the quiet variant used when the board is shown as part of a longer sequence

0xd860.name: wRankingNameRowBuffer
0xd860.note: [7 bytes] Where a ranking name too long for one row is split. RenderPlayerNameFitted measures the name with GetStringLength and, at six characters or more, calls RenderNameTwoRows: RenderNameTopRow copies the first four characters here and appends $2d ('-') and a terminator, RenderNameBottomRow copies the seven bytes from the fifth character on, and each row is then drawn from here by DrawNameWithDiacritics

unions.comment:
Screen-sized buffers in WRAM bank $03 that three unrelated screens keep
at the same addresses, so the variants are scoped to the owning ROM bank.
Bank $3b's copy is the largest and covers the whole span; the other two
sit inside it.

variants.context: created characters and the character grid (bank $38)

0xd900.name: wCreatedCharRecords
0xd900.note: [$c0 bytes] Six $20-byte records for the player-created characters, built by BuildCreatedCharRecords from the save and walked by DrawCreatedCharStats (which seeks with a $20 stride). A record whose first byte is $ff ends the list

0xda00.name: wCharGridEntries
0xda00.note: [$80 bytes] The character-select grid as 32 four-byte entries, cleared when the screen opens and filled by BuildCharUnlockFlags. AddCreatedCharsToCharGrid appends the created characters from $da24 on, four bytes per slot

0xd900.name: wN64RecordsBlock
0xd900.note: [512 bytes] Image of save block $0b, the N64 (Transfer Pak) records, read here by ReadN64RecordsSaveBlock for the trophies screen and the ring-shot and star-victory grids. Same block the bank $03 engine stages at wSaveBlockBuffer in WRAM bank $07 -- this is the screen's own copy

0xda00.name: wEndingSceneStep
0xda00.note: [8-bit] Cleared as the ending sequence enters its third scene and stepped through the scenes that follow

0xda01.name: wScreenSequenceTimer
0xda01.note: [8-bit] Frame counter each PlayScreenSequence* routine runs from 0 to $fa while its screen scrolls, then fades out

unions.comment:
Ring-shot entry list (WRAM bank $03), owned by the bank $3b N64 records
screen and scoped to that bank.

0xdc40.name: wRingShotEntryList
0xdc40.note: [16 bytes] The ring-shot rows to show, copied from the N64RingShot table and then patched: an entry becomes $10 (the blank row) when the matching bit in the N64 records block is clear, so a course the player never transferred is left out

unions.comment: State for a frame task that was stubbed out (WRAM bank $07).

0xdb26.name: wStubbedPromptTaskState
0xdb26.note: [2 bytes] RunStoryDataConfirmMenu selects WRAM bank $07, clears +$00, sets +$01 to $0c and registers StubNop_1b_09 as a per-frame task. That task's body is a bare ret, so nothing ever reads either byte -- the register/unregister pair around the prompt is real, only the work is missing

unions.comment:
The top of WRAM0, shared by two things that never run together: the
serial link's nibble staging and the character-select roster. Scoped to
the owning ROM bank.

0xce40.name: wLinkNibbleBuffer
0xce40.note: [96 bytes] The block being exchanged, one nibble per byte. Both directions refuse a count that would take it past $5f nibbles. UnpackBytesToNibbles fills it from wLinkByteBuffer and PackNibblesToBytes folds it back

0xcea0.name: wLinkByteBuffer
0xcea0.note: [48 bytes] The packed form of the same block -- two nibbles per byte -- which is what the caller reads and writes

0xce40.name: wCharSelectRoster
0xce40.note: [128 bytes] Copy of CharSelectRosterTable, the grid of character ids the select screen and the unlock-debug screen page through. FindCharSelectRosterEntry searches it and DrawCharSelectMugshots walks it

unions.comment:
Mode-local scratch, the first five bytes above $c780. Scoped to the
minigame banks; bank $1b loads its 32-byte character-select nav grid over
the same address and on past the named mode bytes above, so that use has
no symbol it could be given.

0xc7a0.name: wScorePopupSource
0xc7a0.note: [4 bytes] Position the floating score popup starts from, copied out of wBallHistory + 30 by StartScorePopup and stepped by UpdateScorePopup

0xc7a4.name: wMinigameTargetsAltMode
0xc7a4.note: [8-bit] Set at init by Banana Bunch and Fruit Fantasy, the two minigames whose targets deflect the ball rather than absorb it. While it is nonzero UpdateMinigameTarget runs the Alt draw, hit-test and scoring handlers instead of the ordinary ones

unions.comment:
Mode-local scratch above the named mode flags, same rule as the $c780
block: each mode reuses the bytes, so the variants are scoped to the
owning ROM bank and anything outside them stays numeric.

0xc7be.name: wMinigameTargetsActive
0xc7be.note: [8-bit] Set while the target actors are live; UpdateMinigameTargets returns at once when it is clear

0xc7bf.name: wMinigameLastHitCell
0xc7bf.note: [8-bit] Grid cell the ball last bounced off, recorded by the banana-bunch and fruit-fantasy deflection handlers and read back when the hit is scored

0xc7c0.name: wMinigameTargetGrid
0xc7c0.note: [24 bytes] The 3 x 8 target grid, one byte per cell. AreAllTargetsHit passes only when all 24 read 1; ResetTargetGrid clears it a row at a time (+$07, +$0f, +$17 are the row ends)

0xc7be.name: wCharSelectCursorCol
0xc7be.note: [8-bit] Cursor column carried in and out of RunCharacterSelectScreen, so the new-game roster loop resumes where the player left off

0xc7c0.name: wNewGameRosterFields
0xc7c0.note: [8 bytes] Two bytes per starting character (wCharRecordBuffer + 14 and + 12), collected by RunNewGameSetup before the roster is offered

0xc7c8.name: wStoryDataPromptFlag
0xc7c8.note: [8-bit] Cleared by RunStoryDataConfirmMenu as the prompt opens

unions.comment:
The last three bytes of the $c780 mode-local scratch block, which sit
above wTargetZoneEnabled and so need a union of their own. The minigame
target code and the scoreboard both own them, in different modes.

0xc78d.name: wMinigameHitTargetType
0xc78d.note: [8-bit] Type of the target the ball just hit, an index into MinigameTargetTypeScores; $ff means the hit scores nothing

0xc78e.name: wMinigameHitPending
0xc78e.note: [8-bit] Set by the deflect hit-test and cleared by ScoreMinigameTargetHitOrDeflectBall once the hit has been scored

0xc78d.name: wScorePanelValues
0xc78d.note: [3 bytes] Three values SetupScoreboardDisplay draws as 6x2 tile blocks, each fetched through GetTextSlotPointer. The minigame code uses the first two of the same bytes for its hit bookkeeping

unions.comment:
WRAM bank $01 is staging for VRAM, and almost nothing else: every screen
in the game decompresses into it and then QueueVRAMCopies out of it.
What a given offset means therefore depends on what the current screen
put there -- tile graphics, a tilemap plane, its attribute plane -- so
the two halves get names and the offsets do not. Every offset in use is a
whole multiple of TILE_SIZE, which is why they render as tile indices.
Scoped to a provable WRAM bank $01: $d000 is eight different things and
twenty ROM banks stage through this one.
The one overlay with a fixed meaning is bank $1b's character-record copy:
LoadCharacterRecordToBuffer writes $d580 in whichever bank the caller left
selected, and bank $1b selects this one, so the record lands on top of the
staging buffer while the new-game roster is being built.

0xd580.name: wCharRecordBuffer
0xd580.note: [128 bytes] Copy of a character record that LoadCharacterRecordToBuffer takes from wPlayer2MainName, so a caller can read one character's fields without disturbing the live records. +$0b is the id CheckCharacterUnlocked tests against $ff, and RunNewGameSetup reads +$0c and +$0e for each of the four starting characters

0xd000.name: wDecompBuffer
0xd000.note: [2048 bytes] Where DecompressData lands and QueueVRAMCopy reads from. A screen may slice it several ways at once -- the cutscene frame loaders keep six frames at tiles 0, 4, 8, 12, 14 and 16, while the EXP screen puts a tilemap plane at tile 0 and its attributes at tile 64. CopyMapToScrollBuffers reads the map planes back out of it to expand them into WRAM bank $02

0xd800.name: wTextTileBuffer
0xd800.note: [2048 bytes] The other half, where DrawStringToTileBuffer renders a string as tile data rather than as tilemap cells -- the EXP screen's captions and bonus messages are built here and uploaded like any other graphics

unions.comment:
Pre-rendered scoreboard columns for the flipped court, WRAM bank $04.
LoadCourtSceneGraphics copies two $28-byte blocks here out of the scene
record; RefreshCourtScoreboardFlipped feeds them to CopyScoreboardTileColumn,
which reads its source under bank $04 and writes its destination under bank
$02 -- which is why the court planes it writes into are named from a ROM
range rather than a provable WRAM bank.

0xde80.name: wScoreboardColumnTiles
0xde80.note: [40 bytes] Tile half of the scoreboard columns for a court played from the far side. RefreshCourtScoreboardFlipped copies it, and the row 30 bytes in ($de9e), into wCourtTilemapSaved; the middle offset $de94 is the second column it draws.

0xdea8.name: wScoreboardColumnAttrs
0xdea8.note: [40 bytes] CGB attribute half of the same columns, laid out cell for cell with wScoreboardColumnTiles and copied into wCourtAttrmapSaved by the same routine.

unions.comment:
WRAM bank $02 holds tilemap planes, and until now not one byte of it had
a name -- it was the only WRAMX bank with no SECTION at all. Three
subsystems use it three different ways, so $d000 is a tile plane, an
attribute plane or a 64-wide scroll buffer depending on who is asking:
the match keeps the court tilemap and attrmap here as a pair, the
overworld builds two of its four wide scroll planes here, and every
full-screen UI uses $d000 as the attribute half of the tilemap whose
tile half is wShadowTilemap in WRAM bank $03.
Every scope carries wram_bank $02 as well as its ROM bank, and the common
screen case is scoped rather than a default. A default variant here was
the first thing tried and it was wrong twice over: it named the bank $07
save-editor window at $d300 as an attribute cell, and bank $08 reaches
both this bank and WRAM bank $04 -- RefreshCourtScoreboard's $de9x bytes
are not court planes at all.
The match owns the court planes from two more banks, over instruction
ranges rather than whole banks. Bank $06's in-match UI restores and
flushes them: ShowMessageWindow and the pause menu select WRAM bank $02
and then call RestoreBgTilemap / RestoreBgTilemapRegion /
FlushTilemapToVram, which is why $d000 there is the tile half sent to VRAM
bank 0 and not the attribute plane the whole-bank variant below would name
it. Bank $0a's LoadCourtSceneGraphics decompresses the court into the
saved pair at $d800/$dc00 before the match starts.
Bank $0d gets a whole-bank scope like $08's, and it is the one bank that
names all four planes in one routine: LoadMatchUiCourtTilemap pushes the
target-zone overlay's tile and attribute halves twice each and CopyTextRects
them to $d12b, $d92b, $d52b and $dd2b, tiles to the two tilemaps and
attributes to the two attrmaps. QueueMinigameHudVRAMCopy says the same with
the VRAM bank bit: $d120 goes to $9920 and $d520 to $9920 + VRAM_BANK1.

0xd000.name: wCourtTilemap
0xd000.note: [1024 bytes] The court tilemap the match renders from; UploadCourtTilemap sends it to $9800 in VRAM bank 0. Held in WRAM bank $02 rather than the usual $03 because the match owns bank $03 for other things

0xd400.name: wCourtAttrmap
0xd400.note: [1024 bytes] Its CGB attribute plane, cell for cell, uploaded to $9800 in VRAM bank 1 by UploadCourtAttrmap

0xd800.name: wCourtTilemapSaved
0xd800.note: [1024 bytes] Copy of the court tilemap taken when the players change ends. SnapshotCourtTilemaps copies it back over wCourtTilemap to restore the un-flipped view

0xdc00.name: wCourtAttrmapSaved
0xdc00.note: [1024 bytes] The attribute half of the same snapshot

0xd000.name: wMapScrollPlane0
0xd000.note: [1024 bytes] One of the four 64-wide planes CopyMapToScrollBuffers expands the map into, 16 rows of 64 cells. The narrow source comes from wDecompBuffer in WRAM bank $01 through wTextBuffer, a row block at a time

0xd800.name: wMapScrollPlane1
0xd800.note: [1024 bytes] The second plane, built the same way and then immediately cleared -- 2048 bytes of it, twice what was written. wScreenScratch in WRAM bank $03 gets the same treatment, so two of the four planes are assembled and thrown away

0xd000.name: wScreenAttrmap
0xd000.note: [1024 bytes] CGB attributes for the full-screen UIs, cell for cell with wShadowTilemap in WRAM bank $03 -- the pair is what FlushCharDataTilemapChunk sends to $99e0 in VRAM banks 0 and 1. Seventeen ROM banks write cells here, which is why it is the default rather than a scoped variant. The page images the character-data screens patch from sit above it and keep their numeric addresses, being cells in two banks at once. The three bank $1e ranges are the EXP award screen's first argument to a plane writer that selects both banks itself -- FillTilemapRun stores the tile under WRAM bank $03 and the attribute under $02, WriteTextToTilemap and RenderProportionalTextAt likewise -- so at the head of DrawExpTotalPanel, DrawExpMessageWindow and the two message lines of DrawNextExpAwardMessage the live bank is the caller's ($06, or unprovable) and not the operand's. Each of those routines' later cells already render from a provable bank $02, only because FillTilemapRun happens to leave it selected on return

0xd580.name: wCharRecordScratch
0xd580.note:
[128 bytes] The character record a menu is about to draw. LoadCharacterRecordToBuffer asks LoadCharacterRecordToCa80 to build the record and then copies 128 bytes of it here from wPlayer2MainName, so the fields line up with that block: +$0b is the character id (wPlayer2CurrentMainCharacter's offset), which is what CheckCharacterUnlocked tests against $ff and what the mugshot and portrait loaders take as their index. The `.fixedRecord` shortcut writes $3e straight into +$0b without loading anything.
Scoped to instruction ranges rather than a WRAM bank because the bank is never selected at the reference: bank $3b's BuildSaveSlotSummaries is the one caller that says it out loud, running `wram_bank $02` on both sides of the call, and the reads have to be in the bank the write went to.

unions.comment:
Two save-block readers share $d400 in WRAM bank $06. Scoped to the owning
ROM bank as well as the WRAM bank -- bank $1e writes shadow-tilemap cells
at these addresses in WRAM bank $03, which is what a bank-only scope
would have claimed.

0xd400.name: wStorySlotSignatures
0xd400.note: [12 bytes] One wStorySaveSignature per story slot, cached four bytes apart by CacheStorySlotSummaries so CheckStorySignatureCollision can compare a new signature against all three without touching SRAM again

0xd400.name: wUnlockFlagsBlock
0xd400.note: [512 bytes] Image of save block $0b read by ReadUnlockFlagsSaveBlock for the minigame-flags debug screen -- the same block bank $3b stages at wN64RecordsBlock in WRAM bank $03 and the bank $03 engine at wSaveBlockBuffer in bank $07

unions.comment:
Character-select handedness (WRAM bank $03), owned by bank $38. The same
address is the per-character match struct in WRAM banks $04-$07, which is
a different union in different banks.

0xdf00.name: wCharGridHandedness
0xdf00.note: [8-bit] Handedness the exhibition and link character grids are offering for the highlighted character: 0 right, 1 left, 2 not yet chosen. START toggles it with `xor $01` but only when IsMarioCastCharacter passes, and 2 becomes 1 on the first press. DrawCharSelectSlotLabel picks one of three pre-rendered labels off it -- 30:150/151/152, "START: Right-Handed", "START: Left-Handed" and "START: Change Hands". The story-mode screen keeps its own copy at wCharSelectHandedness in WRAM0

unions.comment: Character-grid scroll counter (WRAM bank $03), owned by bank $38.

0xde00.name: wCharGridScrollCount
0xde00.note: [8-bit] Incremented every time the grid scrolls down a row. The select screen prints it as a decimal byte at row 3, column 1 each frame, which makes it a counter left on screen -- there is no other reader

unions.comment:
Chart row store for the bank $3b N64 exhibition and Mario-cast screens
(WRAM bank $03). Sixteen rows of 17 bytes each -- a flag byte and sixteen
cells -- which is $110 in all, so the array actually reaches $dc0f and the
last row runs into the block below. That is why wChartColumnList begins at
$dc01 rather than $dc00.

0xdb00.name: wChartRows
0xdb00.note: [256 bytes, of $110 used] The decoded chart. InitChartRowFlags writes 1 to the head of each of the 16 rows, stepping 17 at a time; BuildN64ExhibResultsGrid and DecodeN64ExhibResultsRow fill the cells behind them from the N64 records block

unions.comment:
Saved character-data stat pages. Three 576-byte slots, each a parallel copy
in WRAM banks $02 and $03 (tiles and CGB attributes), so an address here
names the cell and the selected bank picks the plane. Declared mirrored:
it allocates nothing, because both banks already declare these bytes.

variants.context: character-data stat pages (mirrored across WRAM banks $02/$03)

scopes.note: SlideToMainCharStatPage and its siblings pass the cell to ApplyTilemapPatchList, which writes it under WRAM bank $03 and then $02; the bank live here is $06, the screen's own working set, so the scope names no wram_bank. Every $d7e0-$dea0 operand in the range is one of the six page-slot cells.

0xd7e0.name: wCharDataPageSlot1
0xd7e0.note: [576 bytes] Saved stat page, mirrored across WRAM banks $02/$03 like wCharDataPagePlane. SaveWorkTilemapToPage copies the live screen here when its selector is 2, once per bank; the three 36-byte rows sit 8 * TILEMAP_WIDTH apart and are what MainCharStatPageTilemapPatch* patch through ApplyTilemapPatchList.

0xda20.name: wCharDataPageSlot2
0xda20.note: [576 bytes] Saved stat page, mirrored across WRAM banks $02/$03 like wCharDataPagePlane. SaveWorkTilemapToPage copies the live screen here when its selector is 1, once per bank; the three 36-byte rows sit 8 * TILEMAP_WIDTH apart and are what MainCharStatPageTilemapPatch* patch through ApplyTilemapPatchList.

0xdc60.name: wCharDataPageSlot3
0xdc60.note: [576 bytes] Saved stat page, mirrored across WRAM banks $02/$03 like wCharDataPagePlane. SaveWorkTilemapToPage copies the live screen here when its selector is 0 or 3+, once per bank; the three 36-byte rows sit 8 * TILEMAP_WIDTH apart and are what MainCharStatPageTilemapPatch* patch through ApplyTilemapPatchList.

unions.comment:
Intro-cutscene tilemap planes, WRAM bank $04. Bank $6b decompresses the
cutscene's tile map to $d800 and its CGB attribute map to $dc00, then
QueueVRAMCopies matching offsets to the same VRAM address in banks 0 and 1.
Declared mirrored so it names these bytes without allocating them: the match
engine's ball history, sprite and object slots already declare this range in
WRAM bank $04, and the cutscene simply owns it at a different time.

0xd800.name: wIntroCharactersTilemap
0xd800.note: [1024 bytes] Tile plane of the intro cutscene's character artwork, decompressed here from DataPtr_IntroCharactersTilemap. Rows are TILEMAP_WIDTH apart; the state inits QueueVRAMCopy slices of it ($d880 and $d8c0, 4 and 6 rows in) to $9c80/$9cc0 in VRAM bank 0, pairing each with the same offset of wIntroCharactersAttrmap into VRAM bank 1.

0xdc00.name: wIntroCharactersAttrmap
0xdc00.note: [1024 bytes] CGB attribute plane for wIntroCharactersTilemap, cell for cell, from DataPtr_IntroCharactersAttrmap. Every copy out of it targets VRAM bank 1 at the address its tile-plane twin goes to in bank 0.

unions.comment:
Story-scene record, WRAM bank $06: the $88-byte slot LoadStorySceneGraphics
copies out of the scene table before handing the scene to the overworld engine.

0xdc08.name: wStorySceneRecord
0xdc08.note: [136 bytes] The current story scene's record, copied here from its slot with CopyDataFromBank. The loader reads four bytes at +2 straight back out into wMapScrollMinX, wMapScrollMinY, wMapWidthTiles and wMapHeightTiles, so the first fields are the map's scroll bounds and tile dimensions.

unions.comment:
Staging buffer UpdateSceneTileAnimations ($0a:$6460) assembles the scene's
animated tiles in before queueing them to VRAM. Same subsystem and the same
scope as the $da80 union below, kept separate only because the animation
header starts at $da80 -- which is also what bounds the buffer, since no
length for it appears in the code.

0xd900.name: wSceneTileAnimBuffer
0xd900.note: [at most $180 bytes, bounded by wSceneTileAnimHeader above it] Base of the tile staging buffer. Referenced once, as the initial value of wSceneTileAnimBufferPtr; the bytes are filled by FarCopyBytes through that cursor and read out by QueueVRAMCopy

unions.comment:
Scene tile-animation record, WRAM bank $05: an $88-byte slot InitSceneTileAnimations
copies in before building its animation slots.

0xda80.name: wSceneTileAnimHeader
0xda80.note: [8 bytes] Header of the tile-animation record InitSceneTileAnimations copies from the scene slot; the entry list follows at wSceneTileAnimEntries.

0xda88.name: wSceneTileAnimEntries
0xda88.note: [128 bytes] The scene's tile-animation entries. InitSceneTileAnimations tests the first byte against $fe and skips building any slots when the list is empty.

0xdb10.name: wSceneTileAnimBufferPtr
0xdb10.note: [16-bit] Rolling write cursor into wSceneTileAnimBuffer. UpdateSceneTileAnimations ($0a:$647a) seeds it with the buffer base each pass, reads it back as the FarCopyBytes destination and as the QueueVRAMCopy source, then advances it by the number of bytes copied ($0a:$6571)

0xdb12.name: wSceneTileAnimSrcPtr
0xdb12.note: [16-bit] Far source pointer for the frame being staged, copied two bytes at a time out of the scene's slot 6 record by FarCopyBytes ($0a:$652c), then offset by the frame index before the tile data is fetched

unions.comment:
Window-fit table, WRAM bank $05: four 4-byte entries FitWindowToText indexes
with a window id shifted twice, reading the first word of the entry.

0xd800.name: wWindowFitTable
0xd800.note: [16 bytes] Four 4-byte entries. FitWindowToText turns a window id into an offset with two `sla a` and reads the entry's first word into hl before centring the text against wDialogueWindowWidth / Height. ResetTextWindowState clears it along with the rest of $d800-$dfff in this bank.

unions.comment: Story-scene decompression scratch, WRAM bank $06.

0xd800.name: wStorySceneUnusedBuffer
0xd800.note: [1024 bytes] Third decompression destination of LoadStorySceneGraphics, and the only one nothing lands in: the `ld de, $d800` that selects it is overwritten by the next `ld de, $d400` before any call, so the store is dead. Its two live siblings decompress into $d400 and $d000 of this bank, and the planes after those go to wScreenAttrmap and the bank $03 tilemap.

unions.comment:
Character mugshot staging, owned by bank $1b. LoadCharMugshotToBuffer
decompresses nine tiles here and CopyMugshotBufferToVram queues them into
VRAM bank 1; the pair is always called back to back and nothing between
them selects a WRAM bank, so the buffer lives in whichever bank the calling
screen happens to have mapped -- $02 and $03 within one routine on the
character-select screen, $03 on the trophy and bracket screens, and $04 has
been observed too. Declared mirrored: it allocates nothing, since each of
those banks already declares these bytes.

variants.context: mugshot staging (bank $1b, mirrored across WRAM banks $02/$03/$04)

0xd600.name: wMugshotBuffer
0xd600.note: [144 bytes] One 3 x 3 tile mugshot, decompressed from the entry CharMugshotGfxPointers holds for the character id in a. CopyMugshotBufferToVram sends all nine tiles to the VRAM address its caller passes in de.

unions.comment:
The plane pair whichever screen is running owns, as bank $06's two address
getters see it. GetShadowTilemapAddr and GetShadowAttrmapAddr add a scrolled
cell offset to $d000 / $d400 and hand the result back to a caller that has
already selected the bank: the in-match UI runs them under WRAM bank $02
(the court planes) and the story menus under bank $05 (the window engine's
planes), so no per-bank name fits the literal. Declared mirrored -- both
banks already declare these bytes under their own names, and this is a third
way to address them.
Bank $03 is deliberately left out of the set. It is the third home of a
plane pair (wShadowTilemap / wShadowAttrmap), but nothing observed reaches
these two getters with it selected, and listing it would stop a site proved
to be bank $03 from staying numeric.

variants.context: current screen's plane pair (mirrored across WRAM banks $02/$05)

0xd000.name: wActiveTilemap
0xd000.note: [1024 bytes] BG tile plane of the screen currently running, 32 x 32 cells with rows TILEMAP_WIDTH apart. The same bytes are wCourtTilemap in WRAM bank $02, wWindowShadowTilemap in bank $05 and wShadowTilemap in bank $03; wShadowTilemapBank / wShadowTilemapPtr are how the text engine is told which one is live.

0xd400.name: wActiveAttrmap
0xd400.note: [1024 bytes] Its CGB attribute plane, cell for cell $400 higher -- wCourtAttrmap, wWindowShadowAttrmap or wShadowAttrmap depending on the bank. FlushTilemapToVram sends the tile half to $9800 in VRAM bank 0 and this half to the same address in bank 1.

unions.comment:
The overworld's 64 x 64 cell map buffer: a whole WRAM bank of tile ids in
WRAM bank $03 and the matching CGB attributes in WRAM bank $02, cell for
cell at the same address. The three routines that address it all read the
returned pointer twice, once under each bank -- GetMapBufferAddr64's two
callers copy a row or a column out of $d000 under `wram_bank $02` and then
under `wram_bank $03`, RestoreShadowTilemapRow does the same to rebuild a
row of the window engine's shadow planes, and CopyScrolledSceneTilemapToVram
sends the attribute half to VRAM bank 1 and the tile half to bank 0 -- so
the WRAM bank live at the reference says nothing and the pair of banks is
the name.
Declared mirrored: it allocates nothing, because both banks already declare
these bytes. The bytes it names are the same ones LoadStorySceneGraphics
decompresses into and CopyMapToScrollBuffers fills (wMapScrollPlane0/1 in
WRAM bank $02, wShadowTilemap/wScreenScratch in bank $03), which name
halves of the buffer from the builders' side.

scopes.note: GetSceneTilemapAddr returns base + cell without dereferencing, so no bank is live at the operand; its caller CopySceneTilemapRect selects WRAM bank $02 and copies with a $40 row stride, which is this buffer's geometry

0xd000.name: wMapBuffer64
0xd000.note: [4096 bytes] 64 rows of 64 cells, one plane in *each* of WRAM banks $02 and $03 -- bank $03 the tile half, bank $02 the CGB attribute half. Rows are 64 apart and both axes wrap within the buffer, which is what the `and $3f` on each camera coordinate and the `res 5, h / set 4, h` in BlitBGColumnFrom64 are for. Only the top 32 rows carry map data; CopyMapToScrollBuffers clears the bottom half after building it.
